content.body: Imagine you're a shopkeeper looking at your daily sales. You want to find the best consecutive 3-day period to run a special promotion. How would you quickly find those 3 days with the highest total sales? In this lesson, we'll learn an efficient way to find the maximum sum of any fixed-size window in an array.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:
1. Explain why checking every possible window is inefficient
2. Understand how to use a sliding window to avoid re-scanning
3. Implement the maximum sum subarray algorithm for any window size
4. Recognize when this pattern applies to real-world problems
5. Calculate the time complexity improvement over brute force
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Let's start with a simple example. You have sales data for 4 days: [100, 200, 300, 400]. You want to find the best 2-day period.
content.title: Try it
content.prompt: What's the maximum sum of any 2 consecutive days?
content.successMessage: Great! Days 3 and 4 (300 + 400 = 700) give the highest total.

content.title: Try a bigger array
content.prompt: Now with 6 days: [3, 5, 2, 1, 7, 4]. Find the best 3-day period.
content.successMessage: Well done! Days 4-6 (2 + 1 + 7 = 10) give the maximum sum.

content.title: One more
content.prompt: With 8 days: [2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2, 1, 4]. Find the best 4-day period.
content.successMessage: Excellent! You checked windows until you found days 3-6 (5 + 1 + 3 + 2 = 11).

content.body: What you just did was brute force: you calculated the sum for each possible window by adding all elements in that window. For the 8-day array with 4-day windows, you calculated: 2+1+5+1=9, then 1+5+1+3=10, then 5+1+3+2=11, and so on. Each calculation involved adding k numbers.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When you have 365 days of sales data and want to find the best 30-day period, you'd need to calculate the sum for 336 different windows. Each calculation would add 30 numbers. That's 336 × 30 = 10,080 additions! We need a smarter method that avoids re-adding the same numbers. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Remember what we have already seen. When we move from one window to the next, most of the numbers stay the same! Only one number leaves the window and one new number enters. Instead of re-scanning the entire window, we can keep track of the current sum and just adjust it by subtracting what leaves and adding what enters.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Think of it like a moving train car. You have a fixed number of seats (k). When the train moves forward one station, one passenger gets off (subtract) and one new passenger gets on (add). You don't need to count all the passengers again—just update your count based on who left and who arrived.

content.body: We'll use a sliding window approach with a single pass through the array.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
Let's walk through [2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2], k=3:
1. First window: 2+1+5 = 8 (max=8)
2. Slide right: subtract 2, add 1 → 8-2+1 = 7 (max=8)
3. Slide right: subtract 1, add 3 → 7-1+3 = 9 (max=9)
4. Slide right: subtract 5, add 2 → 9-5+2 = 6 (max=9)
We found max=9 with only 6 additions instead of 12!

content.body:
1. Calculate the sum of the first k elements
2. Set this as your initial maximum
3. Loop through the rest of the array:
   - Subtract the element that's leaving the window
   - Add the new element entering the window
   - Update the maximum if the new sum is larger
4. Return the maximum sum
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up the function
steps.instruction: Create a function called maxSumSubarray that takes an array (arr) and window size (k) as parameters. Return 0 if k is larger than the array length.
steps.hint: Start with the function signature and a guard clause.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function that returns 0 when k > arr.length
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've set up the basic structure with input validation.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost! Don't forget to return 0 when k is too large.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. The function should take arr and k, and return 0 if k > arr.length.

steps.title: Calculate first window sum
steps.instruction: Inside your function, calculate the sum of the first k elements. Store it in a variable called windowSum.
steps.hint: You can use a for loop or slice() with reduce().
steps.expectedOutcome: windowSum contains the sum of arr[0] through arr[k-1]
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! You've calculated the initial window sum correctly.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close! Make sure you're summing exactly k elements starting from index 0.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember to loop from i=0 to i<k and add each arr[i] to windowSum.

steps.title: Initialize maximum sum
steps.instruction: Set the maximum sum (maxSum) to equal the initial windowSum. We'll update this as we slide the window.
steps.hint: Create a variable called maxSum and assign windowSum to it.
steps.expectedOutcome: maxSum variable created with initial window sum
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! Now we have a starting point for tracking the maximum.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost! Don't forget to declare maxSum and set it equal to windowSum.
steps.feedbackWrong: Create a variable maxSum and set it to windowSum's value.

steps.title: Slide the window
steps.instruction: Now loop through the rest of the array. For each position i starting from k, slide the window: subtract the element leaving (arr[i-k]) and add the new element (arr[i]). Update windowSum and maxSum if needed.
steps.hint: Use a for loop where i starts at k and goes to arr.length.
steps.expectedOutcome: Window slides through array, updating sums efficiently
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You're sliding the window and updating the maximum correctly.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close! Make sure you subtract arr[i-k] and add arr[i], then update maxSum.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember: windowSum = windowSum - arr[i-k] + arr[i], then maxSum = Math.max(maxSum, windowSum).

steps.title: Return the result
steps.instruction: Finally, return maxSum from your function.
steps.hint: Add a return statement at the end of the function.
steps.expectedOutcome: Function returns the maximum sum of any k consecutive elements
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! You've implemented the complete sliding window algorithm!
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there! Just add return maxSum; at the end.
steps.feedbackWrong: Don't forget to return the maxSum variable at the end of the function.

content.body:
Congratulations! You've implemented the maximum sum subarray algorithm using a sliding window. Key takeaways:
1. Instead of re-scanning each window, we slide it and adjust the sum
2. We subtract the element leaving and add the new element entering
3. This reduces time complexity from O(n×k) to O(n)
4. The pattern applies to any problem with fixed-size contiguous windows

Remember: The sliding window technique is powerful for array problems where you need to examine contiguous segments efficiently. Keep practicing with different window sizes and array types!
content.title: Done
